frames.narration: A list of 1,000 random items arrives. Sorting it by comparing pairs needs at least about n log2 n comparisons: merge sort takes 8,728.
Insertion sort moves an item one place per comparison, so on the same random list it needs 256,407 comparisons. Quicksort with a first-element pivot needs 12,469: fast here.

Now the same quicksort gets a list that is already sorted. Every pivot is the smallest item, each partition peels off one item, and it needs 499,500 comparisons: the worst case is a property of the input pattern, not of the algorithm alone.
Sorting made the list searchable. Binary search halves the range each probe: about 10 comparisons for 1,000 items, against about 500 on average for a scan.

But the sort cost 8,728 comparisons up front. Each search saves about 490, so sorting first only wins from about 18 searches. The service that answers 100 lookups gains a lot; one that answers 5 loses.
A trap: a helper that re-sorts the list on every one of 100 lookups pays 872,800 comparisons, where sorting once would cost 8,728.
A report needs only the top 10. A min-heap of 10 compares each item with its smallest: 1,171 comparisons for 1,000 random items instead of sorting everything.
Counting sort uses no comparisons, but costs n plus the key range: 67,532 steps when keys reach 65,531, and only 2,010 when there are 10 distinct keys. Pick the sort from the keys, not from habit.
